Agreement between raters, with every measure that should go with it

Source: R/core-stats-agreement.R
hr_agreement.Rd

One call for agreement between two raters on nominal labels, or among any number of coders at a declared level of measurement.

Usage

hr_agreement(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  coders = NULL,
  level = c("nominal", "ordinal", "interval", "ratio"),
  positive = NULL,
  B = 2000,
  conf = 0.95,
  seed = 1
)

Arguments

x

Labels from the first rater, or a matrix or data frame of coders with y left NULL.

y

Labels from the second rater, the same length as x. Read as the reference when positive is given. Items where either is NA are left out, and the result says how many.

coders

A matrix or data frame with items in rows and coders in columns, NA for a missing label. Used in place of x and y.

level

Level of measurement of the labels: "nominal", "ordinal", "interval" or "ratio". Anything but nominal is reported as alpha.

positive

For two raters, the label that counts as positive. Turns on sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV, with y as the reference.

B

Number of bootstrap resamples for the kappa and alpha intervals. 0 skips them.

conf

Confidence level for every interval.

seed

Seed for the bootstrap.

Value

An object of class hr_agreement: a list with type ("two_raters" or "coders"), level, n (items used), dropped (items left out for missing labels), categories, table (the count table for two raters, the coincidence matrix for coders), stats (a data frame with columns statistic, estimate, se, lower and upper), po, kappa, alpha, paradox_flag, positive, notes, conf and bootstrap (B and seed). It has print() and as_json() methods.

Details

Two raters (x and y, nominal). The result holds the count table and, from it:

  • po, the observed agreement, with a Wilson interval;

  • Cohen's kappa, its large-sample standard error (Fleiss, Cohen and Everitt 1969) and a percentile bootstrap interval over items;

  • the prevalence index PI = (a - d) / n and bias index BI = (b - c) / n of Byrt, Bishop and Carlin (1993), for two categories only;

  • PABAK = (k po - 1) / (k - 1) for k categories (2 po - 1 for two), whose interval is the Wilson interval on po mapped the same way;

  • Gwet's AC1 with the variance of Gwet (2008) and a t interval on n - 1 degrees of freedom, held to between -1 and 1;

  • positive and negative specific agreement, 2a / (2a + b + c) and 2d / (2d + b + c), for two categories;

  • when positive is given, y is read as the reference and sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV are reported with Wilson intervals (one category against the rest when there are more than two).

The categories are the labels either rater used. Factor levels that neither rater used are left out, with a note naming them, so a spare level does not change k (and with it PABAK and AC1) or hide PI, BI and specific agreement. The one exception is positive, which stays in the table when it is a declared level, so an all-negative 2x2 stays 2x2. A positive that is neither a declared level nor a used label is an error.

In the table rows are x and columns y. With two categories the first is positive when it is given (otherwise the first level), so a is "both positive", b "x positive only", c "y positive only" and d "both negative".

Kappa is never reported alone. At a low prevalence it moves with the marginals as much as with agreement, so two raters who agree on 95 of 100 items can score a kappa near zero (Feinstein and Cicchetti 1990); AC1 has the opposite weakness, a value near 1 from shared absence. The print method always shows the table and the full set together.

paradox_flag is TRUE when abs(PI) > 0.8, or when po >= 0.8 and kappa <= 0.4. Either marks a table where kappa should not be compared with a kappa from another sample. Both thresholds are heuristics, not cited cut-offs.

Several coders (a matrix or data frame in coders, or in x with y left out; items in rows, coders in columns, NA where a coder did not label an item), or two raters at a level other than nominal. The result is Krippendorff's alpha from the coincidence matrix (Krippendorff 2011) with the difference function of level:

  • nominal: 0 for equal values, 1 otherwise;

  • ordinal: the squared number of values ranked between the two, counting each end as half, (sum of n_g from c to k - (n_c + n_k) / 2)^2;

  • interval: (c - k)^2;

  • ratio: ((c - k) / (c + k))^2.

Only items with at least two values are pairable. Alpha comes with a percentile bootstrap interval over items. Below 30 pairable items, or when every value is the same so that alpha is undefined, alpha is NA and only percent agreement (the share of matching pairs, from the coincidence matrix) is reported, with a note saying why: alpha from a handful of items is too unstable to be read (Hayes and Krippendorff 2007).

Ordinal levels follow the factor levels when the labels are a factor, and sorted order otherwise. When coders' factors carry different level sets (one coder never used "mid" and its factor has only low and high), the levels are merged keeping each coder's order, so low, high and low, mid, high give low, mid, high. Levels that conflict, or that leave the order of two levels open, are an error for the ordinal level. Interval and ratio levels need numeric labels.

The bootstrap runs under seed, so the same data give the same interval every time, and the caller's random state is left as it was.

References

Byrt, T., Bishop, J. and Carlin, J. B. (1993). Bias, prevalence and kappa. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 46(5), 423-429.

Feinstein, A. R. and Cicchetti, D. V. (1990). High agreement but low kappa: I. The problems of two paradoxes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 43(6), 543-549.

Fleiss, J. L., Cohen, J. and Everitt, B. S. (1969). Large sample standard errors of kappa and weighted kappa. Psychological Bulletin 72(5), 323-327.

Gwet, K. L. (2008). Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology 61(1), 29-48.

Hayes, A. F. and Krippendorff, K. (2007). Answering the call for a standard reliability measure for coding data. Communication Methods and Measures 1(1), 77-89.

Krippendorff, K. (2011). Computing Krippendorff's alpha-reliability. University of Pennsylvania, Annenberg School for Communication.

See also

Other statistics: hr_alt_test(), hr_ht_estimate(), hr_ppi(), hr_prop_ci()

Examples

# Two raters on a screening decision, the second as the reference.
screener <- rep(c("keep", "drop", "keep", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
person <- rep(c("keep", "keep", "drop", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
ag <- hr_agreement(screener, person, positive = "keep", B = 200)
ag
#> <hr_agreement> two raters, nominal, 100 item(s)
#> 
#> Counts (rows x, columns y):
#>       y
#> x      keep drop
#>   keep   40    6
#>   drop    9   45
#> 
#>           statistic estimate    se lower upper
#>  observed agreement    0.850    NA 0.767 0.907
#>               kappa    0.700 0.071 0.562 0.838
#>               PABAK    0.700    NA 0.534 0.814
#>                 AC1    0.701 0.071 0.559 0.842
#>    prevalence index   -0.050    NA    NA    NA
#>          bias index   -0.030    NA    NA    NA
#>  positive agreement    0.842    NA    NA    NA
#>  negative agreement    0.857    NA    NA    NA
#>         sensitivity    0.816    NA 0.686 0.900
#>         specificity    0.882    NA 0.766 0.945
#>                 PPV    0.870    NA 0.743 0.939
#>                 NPV    0.833    NA 0.713 0.910
#> 
#> Intervals at 95%; bootstrap B = 200, seed 1.
#> Positive label: keep; y is the reference.

# Three coders, one item each left blank, ordinal labels.
set.seed(4)
truth <- sample(1:4, 40, replace = TRUE)
codes <- sapply(1:3, function(j) pmin(4, pmax(1, truth + sample(-1:1, 40, TRUE,
                                                              c(0.1, 0.8, 0.1)))))
codes[cbind(1:3, 1:3)] <- NA
hr_agreement(coders = codes, level = "ordinal", B = 200)
#> <hr_agreement> 3 coders, ordinal, 40 pairable item(s)
#> 
#> Coincidence matrix:
#>    1  2  3  4
#> 1 25  3  1  0
#> 2  3  7 10  0
#> 3  1 10 23  4
#> 4  0  0  4 26
#> 
#>             statistic estimate se lower upper
#>     percent agreement    0.692 NA    NA    NA
#>  Krippendorff's alpha    0.858 NA 0.739 0.924
#> 
#> Intervals at 95%; bootstrap B = 200, seed 1.
